Then the slurping started. Grandfather Tanaka slurped. Kenta slurped. Even quiet little Suki, who was only seven, drew her noodles in with a sound like a small wave. Emilia froze with her chopsticks halfway to her mouth. At her own table her father gave one look to anyone who made noise while eating, and her grandmother's memoir of growing up on a farm had a whole chapter about manners, including a line she had read aloud at Thanksgiving: "A quiet table is a polite table." Emilia had always believed that. Now she was not so sure.

She decided to verify it, quietly, like a science experiment. She waited until Grandfather slurped again, and she watched every face around the table. Nobody frowned. Nobody glanced at him. Kenta's mother refilled his tea and smiled. If slurping were rude here, Emilia reasoned, someone would react, the way her father's eyebrows reacted at home. Then she tried the smallest test she could manage: one noodle, drawn in quickly. It made a gentle sound, and Grandmother Tanaka nodded at her and said, "Good, good," and slid the plate of egg closer to her side.

"Better flavor when it's loud," Kenta whispered, leaning toward her. "That's how we do ramen. And soba too." Emilia slurped again, longer this time, and the noodles actually did taste better, hot and quick instead of cooled and slow.

When the bowls were empty, Suki climbed into Emilia's lap and asked whether America still had volcanoes that were extinct. Emilia said most of them were, but a few were only sleeping, and Suki found that so funny she laughed until she hiccupped. Grandmother Tanaka pointed at Emilia's bowl, then at the teapot, and raised her eyebrows. Emilia held out her cup with both hands, the way the candy had been accepted, and watched the tea pour.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: In a blind test, participants do not know which sample is which, so their expectations cannot sway their answers.
story:
Sara set two cereal boxes on the kitchen table, then slid them behind the bread maker where nobody could see the labels. Her science fair project was due Friday, and she had one evening left to prove her idea. "Marcus," she called, "I need you in here. Bring your honest face."

Her brother wandered in with a granola bar hanging out of his mouth. Sara took it away from him. "You're a participant now. No snacks before the test." She poured the name-brand flakes into a bowl marked A and the store-brand flakes into a bowl marked B, then shuffled the boxes deeper behind the bread maker so even she could forget which bowl was which. She copied a code onto a folded slip of paper, taped it shut, and set a heavy mug on top of it.

"What's the mug for?" Marcus asked, dropping into a chair.

"So I can't peek. It's a blind test. You don't know which sample is which, so what you expect can't sway your answers." She slid the bowls toward him with a glass of water between them. "Taste A. Swish. Tell me what you think. Then B. No guessing which is the fancy one."

Marcus chewed slowly, like the flakes might lie to him. "A is crispier," he said. "B tastes a little like the box."

Sara wrote it down. That was the answer she had predicted, and it bothered her. She had guessed her brother would pick A because he always begged for the name-brand stuff, the kind with the artisan bakery logo on the front that made everything sound handmade and expensive. If he couldn't tell the boxes apart and still picked A, maybe his tongue actually knew something. She made him repeat the test with fresh pours, swapping the bowls' positions. Again he chose A.

Then Dad wandered through and Sara made him sit down too. He tasted both, tapped the table, and pointed at B. "That one's better. Toastier."

Sara sat back. Two tasters, opposite answers, and no boxes in sight. She unfolded the slip under the mug and stared at the code. Bowl A was the store brand. Marcus had picked the cheap cereal twice, without knowing it, and praised it. Dad had picked the expensive one. Her prediction had been wrong in the most interesting way possible: people's expectations couldn't sway their answers because people didn't know which sample was which, so the answers were all over the place. Taste, not labels, was doing the talking.

She wrote "Trial Three" at the top of a fresh data sheet and looked up at her father. "Dad, there's water in the glass for a reason. You have to do it again."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Oliver sat on the bench outside the pretzel shop with his phone and one bar of wifi, trying to isolate the reason his sister's old blog had vanished. The link she'd sent him was dead. "It just says page not found," he said.

"Exactly," said Dani, dropping onto the bench beside him with her backpack. She worked at the mall on Saturdays, restocking candy, and she wanted a promotion to the register, which meant she needed to prove the candy store's website had once advertised a free-sample policy that the manager now denied. "If I can show him the old page, I get the register. If I can't, I stay on the candy cart."

"But the page is gone," Oliver said.

"Gone isn't the same as deleted," Dani said. She tapped his screen. "Try the Wayback Machine."

He typed it in. A page loaded with a little carousel icon and a place to enter a web address. "It says the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages since 1996," he read. He put in the candy store's address. A timeline appeared, a row of dates going back years. He picked one from two summers ago, and the old page bloomed on his screen, faded colors and all. Right there, in green letters: free sample with every visit.

"You're a candidate for sainthood," Dani said, photographing his screen with her own phone.

Oliver barely heard her. He had typed in his sister's blog address on a hunch. A date appeared. He clicked it, and the dead page came back to life, every post, every photo. There was his own face at nine years old, in front of their old house, and under it his sister had written the street name and the school he attended. Anyone in the world could be looking at this right now. Any stranger. He scrolled down and found a post with the mall tagged, the very bench he was sitting on, dated three years back.

"Your sister should take that down," Dani said, reading over his shoulder.

"She can't take it down," Oliver said slowly, testing the idea as he said it. "It's not on her site anymore. It's saved somewhere else, and that place lets anyone look." He tried closing his sister's blog and typing the address again. Same result. The copy was just there, patient as a filing cabinet.

He texted his sister a screenshot. Then he looked at his own account settings, the ones that let his posts carry the mall's location without asking him, and switched that off, one toggle at a time.

Dani was already walking toward the candy store with her phone held up like a ticket. "Wish me luck," she called.

Oliver's phone buzzed. His sister had replied with three wide-eyed emojis and one line: "Delete it. Delete everything."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
Maya had one job at the Vaisakhi celebration at the cultural center: hold the front banner during the procession through the parking lot. Her cousin Simran had held it last year, and Maya envied her for it, because the banner carrier got to stand right beside the drummers. But this year the aunties had made a rule. The banner went to whoever won the history game at the kids' table, and Maya had been stuck serving langar when the game started.

By the time she reached the table, her little brother Arjun was already there, frowning at a question card. "I can't get this one," he said. "It's about why Vaisakhi matters."

The volunteer running the table shook her head. "You get two tries. Then the next person goes."

Maya leaned over Arjun's shoulder. The card asked what happened on Vaisakhi, and when, and where. She didn't know all of it. She had heard the words Khalsa and Anandpur before, at the gurdwara, but the pieces wouldn't line up. She couldn't see the answer directly, so she decided to test an idea: the story had to be somewhere in the room, because the whole day was built around it.

"Come on," she said to Arjun. They walked toward the courtyard, where the procession was forming. A small boy tugged on the sleeve of Maya's uncle, who was tying an orange flag to a pole. "Why does everybody make such a big deal about today?" the boy asked.

"Because on Vaisakhi, in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," her uncle said, still working on the flag.

"Which part is the answer?" Arjun whispered. He had only caught half of it.

"Think," Maya said. "What did you already have on your card?" Arjun said the card mentioned a year and a place. The year had to be 1699, because that was when the Guru founded the Khalsa, and the place had to be Anandpur, because that was where it happened. The rest, the part about Guru Gobind Singh being the tenth Guru, filled in the blank about who did it. Maya checked it against the banner itself, which had the words "Khalsa" stitched in gold thread beside a picture of the Punjabi countryside, and against a display of migratory birds painted on the courtyard wall, labeled with routes people had walked from Anandpur over the centuries. Everything matched.

They went back to the table. Arjun read his answer out loud, and the volunteer nodded. Then she turned to Maya. "Your turn. Same question, different card."

Maya took a breath and said it straight: on Vaisakhi, in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur. The volunteer handed her the banner pole.

"Wait," Arjun said. "I won too."

"There's one banner and two of you," the volunteer said. "Work it out."

Maya offered a quick negotiation: she would carry the banner for the first loop around the parking lot, and Arjun could take it when they passed the drummers the second time. Arjun stuck out his hand and they shook on it.

The drums started. Maya lifted the pole high, the orange cloth catching the wind, and stepped out in front.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
Easton slid the box across the kitchen table until it bumped his milk glass, because if he was going to open it, he wanted to do it slowly enough to remember. Inside was his first phone, dark blue, with a case his mom said was durable enough to survive being dropped off a roof. He turned it on while his little sister Priya leaned her elbows on the table and breathed directly on his shoulder.

"Screen time rules," his mom said, sliding the charger across like a business deal. "Homework first, phone in the kitchen at nine. And you have to let me enroll you in the family safety thing tonight." She said it lightly, but she watched his face while she said it, and he nodded because he meant it.

The first thing he wanted was a flashlight app, since his room's ceiling light flickered like it was trying to quit. He found one with a cartoon bulb icon, tapped Install, and stopped. A box had come up. The app wanted permission to use his camera, his microphone, and all of his contacts. Easton frowned at it. "Why would a flashlight need to hear me?" he asked the kitchen.

"To hear if you're scared of the dark," Priya said solemnly.

He didn't tap Allow. Instead he hunted through Settings, tapping into Apps, then Permissions, because his cousin Malik had once said something Easton only half remembered, something about controlling what apps could touch. What he found surprised him: a list. Camera. Microphone. Contacts. Little toggles beside each one, all off. He tested it. He granted the flashlight permission to the camera, then took it away again with one tap, and the toggle went dark. So apps had to ask first, and he could take the permission back later, anytime, right there in the settings.

He tried two more apps to be sure. A drawing app asked for nothing. A free game asked for contacts, microphone, camera, and something about his location. He denied everything, and the game still worked. "Interesting," he said.

"What's interesting?" his mom asked, coming back with two mugs, setting the cocoa one in front of Priya first.

"The flashlight wanted my contacts. Why does a flashlight need to know Priya's friend Gabby's phone number?"

His mom laughed into her mug. "Maybe the bulb wants pen pals." Then she put her hand briefly on his shoulder, the way she did when he did something right without being told. "Take the permission away, then. You know how now."

He did, one tap, and the flashlight turned on anyway, a clean white beam across the table that made Priya's cocoa steam glow like a tiny ghost.

"It works without asking for anything else," Easton said. "So all that asking was just an illusion, like the app was being polite when it was really just being nosy."

"Like Malcolm at recess," Priya said, and both of them cracked up, because Malcolm asked everyone's business and called it journalism.

At nine that night, the phone went in the kitchen drawer, screen glowing through the gap one last time before it slept.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard said 11:52, and Piper had already packed her bag. Three days in Marsh Creek and she knew exactly two people's names, both of which she had learned by reading the sticky labels on their desks. She had inherited her grandmother's habit of arriving early and leaving exactly on time, but today she slowed down, because the girl in the second row, Marisol, was still copying homework.

"Lunch?" Piper asked. It came out flatter than she meant.

Marisol shrugged. "Sure."

At the table, Marisol talked about the soccer team and a teacher everyone called the Reptile. Piper laughed in the right places. When the bell rang, Marisol said, "See you," and walked off toward the gym without looking back. Piper sat alone with her tray for a second, then dumped it.

That night she found the article her history teacher had assigned, a stack of photocopied pages about friendship research. She read one line three times: a 2018 study by Jeffrey Hall of the University of Kansas found that it takes about 50 hours together to turn an acquaintance into a casual friend. Fifty hours. She did the math on her notebook cover. One lunch was thirty-five minutes. Fifty hours was like eighty-five lunches, almost a whole school year of them, and that was only to reach casual.

So she stopped waiting for friendship to happen and started building it like a project. She sat with Marisol every day. She showed up at soccer practice with water bottles. She kept a tally in the back of her notebook, small pencil marks, five minutes at a locker, forty at lunch, ninety at a Saturday game. By the third week she had eleven hours and a pretty good idea of which jokes worked.

Then Marisol grabbed the notebook to borrow a pen and the pages fell open. She stared at the tally marks.

"What is this?"

"Nothing. A count."

"You're counting our hangouts?" Marisol's voice went sharp enough that two girls at the next table turned around. "Am I homework?"

Piper's face went hot. "It's not like that. It's a thing I read. Acquaintances aren't friends yet, that's all. There's a, a number of hours." Even she could hear how it sounded.

Marisol dropped the notebook on the table and left. Piper erased the tally that night, every mark, until the paper was gray and soft. She left the count alone but kept sitting at the table anyway, because the hours didn't care whether she tracked them.

Two weeks later, her mom sent her to the pharmacy to pick up her little brother's antibiotic, and Marisol was at the counter, waiting on a prescription of her own.

"Middle aisle," Marisol said, tilting her head toward the candy. "They still have the sour ones."

Piper followed her. Marisol tore open the bag outside and held it out without a word, and Piper took one, and they walked home the long way, arguing about whether the sour ones were actually better than the chocolate.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
The propane stove clicked three times before it caught, and Thomas set the heavy pan over the blue flame with the confidence of someone who had watched exactly four cooking videos that afternoon. He had promised his family caramel apples for the last night of the camping trip, and the bag of sugar sat beside him like a dare. His little sister Maya dragged her camp chair close enough to be a hazard.

"Is that how the roast got brown this morning?" she asked, nodding at the pan. "Same thing?"

Thomas started to say yes, then stopped. The roast had browned with nothing but its own juices, no sugar anywhere. This was just sugar, alone in the pan. Something felt different about the two, and he wanted to figure out what before he answered her.

"The roast had meat juices," he said slowly, watching the sugar begin to melt at the edges. "There's no meat juice in here. Only sugar." He turned the flame down a notch, because the videos had all warned him about burning, and tried an experiment in his head. If the two brownings were the same thing, they should need the same ingredients. But sugar alone was browning right now, and the roast had browned without any added sugar. So the reactions couldn't be identical. He remembered a word from one of the videos, half-buried under the instructor's terrible jokes: caramelization. That was this, the browning that happened when sugar alone was heated.

"So what was the roast doing?" Maya asked.

"There was another one," Thomas said. "The Maillard reaction. It also needs amino acids." He pointed at the pan. "This is just sugar. No amino acids in here, so no Maillard, just caramelization."

Maya squinted at the melting sugar as if she could see the difference, which of course nobody could. That was the strange part, Thomas thought. Two brownings that looked alike and happened for different hidden reasons, like two endangered animals that look the same until a scientist counts the stripes. You had to reason it out from what went in.

The sugar went amber, then copper. Thomas swirled the pan and listened to Maya narrate like a sports announcer for what she called the Caramel Dynasty, rulers of all desserts. Then the color deepened too fast, and he yanked the pan off the heat with a clatter.

"Too dark?" Maya asked.

"A little." He stirred it, and the burnt edge mellowed into something smoky but still sweet. Not perfect, but not ruined. He dipped one apple slice, held it out, and waited while she bit down.

"Crispy," she declared, mouth full. "The Dynasty lives."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked

fact: PolitiFact, a US fact-checking website founded in 2007, rates claims on a scale it calls the Truth-O-Meter, from True to Pants on Fire.
story:
The meatloaf was still steaming when Dad turned up the TV volume so they could hear the ad over the sound of forks. "Nine out of ten dentists recommend this toothpaste," a deep voice announced, "and studies show it fights cavities better than any other brand." Dad snorted. "Sure they do." But Hailey's little brother Ben swallowed a whole piece of broccoli just to talk faster. "Grandma says that brand is the best one. She read it somewhere." Hailey put down her fork. "Grandma thinking it's the best is her opinion. The ad saying it beats every other brand is different. That's like... you could actually check it." Ben rolled his eyes so hard she could practically hear it.

"That's not different," he said. "It's all just what people think." Dad carried his plate to the counter, chewing the end of a thought, and Hailey noticed he did that whenever he was actually listening. "Your sister has a point," he said. "One you can look up. Her arthritis prescription says something similar on the information sheet, and the pharmacist had actual study numbers behind it. That's a claim with evidence." Hailey grabbed Dad's phone off the counter, careful of the gravy smudge, and typed in the toothpaste claim while the kitchen still smelled of onions and burnt edges.

The results loaded slowly, the way they always did at the far end of the table. Then she found it: a fact-checking site called PolitiFact, founded in 2007, that rates claims people make in politics and ads. "They call their rating scale the Truth-O-Meter," she said, reading aloud. "It goes from True all the way to a rating called Pants on Fire." Ben laughed so hard milk came out of his nose, which ruined the tablecloth Mom had just washed.

But Hailey wasn't laughing. She scrolled, and there it was, a toothpaste study claim from a few years back rated Pants on Fire, because the "nine out of ten dentists" survey had asked dentists to pick from a list that company itself had made. The word "plausible" appeared in the write-up, and it fit exactly: the ad sounded plausible, but it fell apart when someone checked. "Ben," she said, "Grandma's opinion is that it tastes good. That can't be wrong because it's hers. But this company said their study proved something, and PolitiFact could refute it with the actual survey." She slid the phone across the table so the bright screen stopped right beside his plate.

Ben wiped his nose with his sleeve and stared at the little cartoon of pants literally on fire. Then he picked up his fork, jabbed a piece of meatloaf, and said, "Grandma's going to be mad." Hailey was already dialing.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel.
story:
The food bank shared a basement with the public library, which meant Aria had walked past its door a hundred times without ever going in. Today she went in, signed the volunteer sheet, and was handed an empty crate.

"Sort cans by type," said Marcus, the other volunteer, a boy from her school who had been coming since September. "Soup, fruit, pasta, beans. Mrs. Okafor will check it after."

Aria worked fast, but something bothered her. The shelf marked SOUP had a gap in the middle, clean and square, as if someone had lifted out exactly twelve cans in a neat block. The shelves on either side were packed tight. She checked the fruit shelf. Another square gap. Pasta, same thing.

"Inventory already counted this morning," Marcus said when she pointed at it. "Don't worry about it."

But she couldn't stop thinking about it during break. The break room had a corkboard, a microwave, and a framed poster on the wall about the history of food banks. She read it twice. The first food bank, St. Mary's Food Bank in Phoenix, Arizona, was started in 1967 by John van Hengel. The idea had spread from there, all the way down to this basement under the library.

"John van Hengel," Marcus said behind her, reading over her shoulder. "That's the name on the big plaque upstairs, by the donation box."

Aria went still. The donation box. A square box, big enough to hold twelve cans in a neat block. She climbed the stairs, crossed the library's quiet carpet, and found the box by the front desk. It was empty, but the floor around it held a scatter of dust and one dried bean. Somebody had been taking the donated cans before they ever reached the basement. The gaps hadn't evaporated on their own. They had been lifted out, whole squares of them, by someone who knew the box wasn't watched in the afternoons.

She stood where she could see the box and the reading chairs at the same time, pretending to browse, and waited through what felt like the least leisurely leisure reading of her life. After twenty minutes an eccentric old man in a rain hat, though the sky was clear, shuffled over, lifted a square of cans from the box, and slid them into a shopping bag.

"Excuse me," Aria said, louder than she meant to. "Those go downstairs. To the food bank."

"The food bank has plenty," the man said, not slowing down.

"They don't. I just sorted what's left, and there isn't much."

He stopped. He looked at the bag, then at her, then at the plaque on the wall. He read it slowly, moving his lips. "Started in 1967," he murmured. "By John van Hengel. One man. Huh." He set the bag down on the desk. "Take them down, then. I'll carry the second trip."

Aria grinned and picked up the bag. "Race you to the stairs."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A checkable claim can be false; 'The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin' is a wrong factual claim, not an opinion.
story:
Madison set the mashed potatoes down hard enough to rattle the salt shaker. Her little brother Theo had ruined her whole afternoon, and now she had to sit through dinner pretending everything was fine.

"Pass the green beans," Theo said, mouth already full.

"After what you did today? You told everyone in class the Eiffel Tower is in Berlin."

Dad looked up from his plate. Mom stopped cutting her chicken.

"It's my opinion," Theo said. "You can't argue with somebody's opinion. That's what Mr. Randall says. Respect the opinion."

Madison gripped her fork. She had replayed the moment all through last period, her face hot while kids snickered. She wanted to prove him wrong, but she wasn't sure how to fight a word like opinion. It seemed like a shield you could hide anything behind. She pushed a bean around her plate, thinking so hard she barely tasted her food.

"But it's not an opinion," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud the way she'd test a loose tooth. "Pineapple pizza tasting good is an opinion. Nobody can check that. But the Eiffel Tower being in Berlin, that's something you can look up. You can find the tower, find the city, and see they don't match." She pointed her fork at him. "It's still a claim even though it's wrong. It's just a wrong claim."

"That's a hard shot," Dad said, half smiling.

Theo slumped. "So my report is a wrong claim?"

"Your whole poster," Madison said. She remembered the glitter he had used, three evenings of it, and felt a small sting under her victory. He had been proud of that poster.

Mom cleared her throat. "Well, since we're being careful with facts, we need to talk about the science curriculum money. The school board wants to cut the wetland field trips to conserve funds." She and Dad started trading worried numbers, and Madison let their voices wash past her while she watched Theo. He was quietly moving his beans into a pile, not eating them.

Later, while Mom loaded the dishwasher, Madison found Theo's crumpled poster in the trash can by the back door. The Eiffel Tower stood in silver glitter above the word BERLIN, and along the border he had drawn a flock of migratory birds flying south, because his teacher had said every city poster needed one real fact about the place. He had gotten that part right, at least. She smoothed the paper against her knee, thinking she might help him fix the tower part tomorrow, if he'd let her.

She carried the poster upstairs and taped it above his desk, glitter flaking onto the carpet. When Theo came in and saw it, he stood in the doorway for a long moment.

"Paris," he said finally. "It's in Paris."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: One of the first written guides to online manners, 'Netiquette Guidelines', was published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855.
story:
Grace watched the class group chat blow up during lunch. Someone named DragonRider42, who had to be Marcus because he never shut up about dragons, had typed "SURE. WHATEVER." at Priya after she suggested a meeting time for the history project. Priya had replied with three sad faces and then gone silent. Now half the chat thought Marcus was furious, and the other half thought Priya was overreacting, and Mrs. Okafor had already posted "We will discuss this tomorrow."

The problem was that nobody could tell what anyone meant. Grace scrolled back through the messages. Marcus used all caps for everything, even "GOOD MORNING." Priya used exclamation points the way some people waved. And a kid named Devon had typed just "k" an hour ago, which somehow made the whole thread feel desolate, like a hallway after the last bell. Same chat, same words, but each person carried a different tone into it, and the tone vanished the moment they hit send. That was the hidden thing Grace wanted to catch.

She hypothesized that the trouble wasn't the people. It was the missing signals. In person, Marcus said "sure, whatever" in a joking drawl and Priya laughed. Online, the drawl disappeared, leaving only the skeleton of the words. If she could prove that, then the fix wasn't apologies. The fix was rules that put the signals back.

After school she found Marcus at his locker and read his own message out loud in his exact joking voice. "Sure. Whatever." He grinned. "That's how I meant it. I say everything like that." Then she read it flat and cold, the way Priya must have heard it, and his grin faded. "Oh," he said. "That sounds terrible."

That night Grace searched whether anyone had ever bothered to write down official online manners, because it seemed like the kind of problem adults would have noticed decades ago. They had. One of the first written guides to online manners was called the Netiquette Guidelines, published in 1995 as a document called RFC 1855. She sat back. That was older than her parents' marriage. People had been fighting about all caps since before she was born.

The next morning she got to Mrs. Okafor first. "Can I set the rules for the chat?" she asked. "There's a real thing to base it on. One of the first written guides to online manners was published in 1995, a document called RFC 1855." Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "You looked that up?" "Last night. It has a principle I like. Assume the reader can't hear your voice, so don't send anything your face wouldn't survive."

Marcus posted an apology before homeroom, in normal lowercase, and Priya answered with a thumbs-up and "thanks!" with the exclamation point, which Grace now knew was Priya's wave. At the end of the period Grace added one line to the pinned rules: if you mean it as a joke, say so out loud someday, where people can hear you smile.

She clicked the pin, and the little gray flag appeared beside the rules.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: Psychologist John Suler described the 'online disinhibition effect' in 2004: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face.
story:
Mia had never said a rude word to anyone, as far as Victoria knew. She held doors, she thanked the lunch ladies, she even complimented people's braces. So when Victoria opened the comments under the science fair photos and saw "nice volcano, did a preschooler make it," signed with Mia's username, she read it three times. Then she walked straight to the computer lab after last period.

She printed the page, folded it, and found Mia by the water fountain the next morning. "Did you write this?" she asked, holding it out.

Mia looked at the paper, and her face went pale. "It was supposed to be a joke," she said quietly. "People say stuff like that online all the time. It doesn't count."

"It counts to me," Victoria said. She watched Mia's hands shake a little, and she noticed something odd: Mia could not even look at the comment, as if reading it out loud in a hallway made it too real. Victoria walked away without an answer, because she didn't have the right question yet.

At home she searched the words from her own experience: why do nice people write mean comments online. The third result changed everything. A psychologist named John Suler had described it back in 2004 and called it the online disinhibition effect: people often say things online that they would hold back from saying face to face. Victoria leaned closer to the screen. That was it, exactly. The screen was a private space even when the whole world could see it, and Mia's politeness in the crowded hallway was the public version of her, a complete contradiction living in one person.

Victoria tested her idea the next day, carefully, like a real experiment. She posted a reply to the comment: "Would you say this to my face at school? If yes, meet me at lunch." She sat at her usual table at noon and waited, her tray in front of her, her stomach doing flips. The cafeteria noise seemed to dissolve when Mia appeared at the end of the table, holding her own tray, not sitting down yet.

"I couldn't sleep," Mia said. "I kept imagining you reading it alone in your room." She set her tray down across from Victoria. "I'd never say it out loud. Not to anyone. I don't know why the typing made it feel like it wasn't me." She pulled a folded paper from her pocket, the printout of her comment, and tore it in half. "Can I fix it? I already wrote a new comment saying the volcano was actually great, and that I'm sorry. Want to check it before I post it?"

Victoria slid her chair over so they could read it together on Mia's phone, side by side at the lunch table, where everything was face to face.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Losing about 2 percent of body weight in sweat without drinking enough can noticeably reduce athletic performance, especially in endurance events.
story:
The bleachers were still cold at seven in the morning, and Nolan sat on the third row lacing his shoes while the distance coach clicked her stopwatch. Today was the day. One mile, four laps around the track, and the seven fastest boys would make the cross country team. Nolan had run this mile in his head so many times that the laps had almost worn grooves in his imagination.

Marcus Delgado was stretching by the fence, and he was doing something strange. When Nolan's friend Priya offered him her water bottle, Marcus waved it away. "Water makes you heavy," Marcus said. "I haven't drunk anything since last night. I want to be light."

Something about that tickled a memory in Nolan. Last summer their landlord, Mr. Okafor, had jogged past their apartment every morning carrying a water bottle nearly the size of a fire extinguisher, even on days when it wasn't hot. Nolan had once asked him why he bothered, and Mr. Okafor had only shrugged and said, "The scale in the basement tells me." At the time Nolan had thought he was joking about his weight. Now he wasn't so sure.

There was an old doctor's scale in the locker room, the kind with sliding weights. The day before tryouts, Nolan had done a strange experiment. He had weighed himself, run two miles in the afternoon heat without drinking anything, and weighed himself again. Ninety-two pounds before, about ninety before. Two pounds gone, which was roughly two percent of him, and it had all left through his shirt, which was soaked. That evening he had felt like a wrung-out dish towel. He tried to replicate the run the next morning with a bottle of water, and although the sweat was the same, his legs on the last half mile had felt entirely different. Light without water, it turned out, was not the same as strong.

"Are you going to drink or just stare at that bottle?" Priya asked. She was trying out too, for the girls' heat after theirs.

"Drinking," Nolan said, and did. It felt strange to be doing the exact opposite of his fastest rival, based mostly on a landlord, a locker room scale, and one afternoon of feeling terrible. Maybe Marcus was right. Maybe Nolan was about to be the slowest well-hydrated boy in the seventh grade.

The coach blew her whistle, and the eight boys took off. Marcus led from the gun, and by the end of the second lap he was five meters clear, running so smoothly that part of Nolan wanted to just watch him. But this was the longest race most of them had ever run, and a mile is an endurance event whether it looks like one or not. On the third lap Marcus's shoulders started to climb toward his ears. On the back curve of the fourth, his stride shortened, and the gap began to close all by itself, like a door swinging back on a slow hinge. Nolan passed him with a hundred meters left, and Marcus made a sound somewhere between a groan and a whimper, which was more eloquent than any speech about how he felt.

Afterward Marcus sat on the infield grass, gray-faced, while Priya held out the water bottle he had refused. He took it this time. "Two percent," Nolan heard himself say, and then he stopped, because the coach was calling out the names, and his was fourth on the list. Priya grinned at him from the fence, and behind her, out on the sidewalk, an old man jogged past with a enormous water bottle, waving.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Going from 40 percent to 50 percent is a rise of 10 percentage points but a 25 percent increase, so the two phrases describe the same change.
story:
Bentley had promised his history teacher he would bring in two news articles about the same poll, and it was already eight o'clock. He sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with his laptop balanced on a couch cushion, because the coffee table had been claimed by his little sister's domino rally, a durable tower of plastic pieces that she guarded like a dragon.

The first article said support for the new park had jumped from 40 percent to 50 percent, a rise of 10 percentage points. The second article, about the exact same poll, called it a 25 percent increase. Bentley read both headlines three times, then flopped backward onto the rug and groaned loudly enough that his sister peeked over her dominoes.

"Someone's wrong," he told the ceiling. "Ten and twenty-five can't both be right."

"You're wrong all the time," his sister said, placing a domino with surgical care.

"Thank you." He could not postpone this. The assignment was due first period, and he had already skipped his math tutor session that afternoon to finish a book report, which his tutor would hear about and find hilarious. He pulled out a notebook and wrote both numbers down like they were suspects in a lineup.

He tried it as a story problem. If forty kids out of a hundred wanted the park, and now fifty did, that was ten more kids. Ten more out of the original forty, though. He circled it, crossed it out, circled it again. Both writers were describing the same change, just in different words, one measuring the whole road and one measuring the hill climbed on it. He sat up so fast he nearly knocked over the domino rally, and his sister shrieked and threw a sock at him.

"Ten percentage points," he said, holding up one finger, "and a twenty-five percent increase. Same change. Both headlines are telling the truth."

"That's the dumbest true thing I've ever heard," she said.

"It's the best thing I've ever heard." He wrote his paragraph at top speed, quoting both articles, and read it aloud once, grinning at the part where he called the two headlines "twins wearing different jackets." His mother called from the kitchen that it was bedtime in ten minutes. Bentley saved the file, closed the laptop, and helped his sister line up the final domino.

"Okay," he said, finger hovering. "On three."
